name: Recoil
summary: Push the player back a little every time they fire, so each shot has some force behind it.
what_it_does: A shot that leaves the gun while nothing happens to the shooter feels like a toy. A short push opposite the aim direction on each shot makes the weapon feel strong, and with rapid fire the pushes add up, so firing nonstop has a cost. In his talk "The art of screenshake", Jan Willem Nijman of Vlambeer adds player knockback while shooting as one of the steps that turn a flat shooter into a punchy one, alongside screen shake and camera kick.
use_when: Shooters, and any weapon that should feel heavy. Make it bigger for big guns and tiny or zero for fast, light ones.
watch_out: Too much push throws off aim and can shove players into hazards or off ledges. Apply it as a velocity that wears off, not a jump in position, and keep it small where the platforming needs precision.
starting_values: No checked source gives a number. Start with a push of 50 to 150 px/s per shot that wears off within about a tenth of a second, then tune it per weapon.
prompt:
Add recoil to shooting.
- When the player fires, add 120 px/s of horizontal velocity opposite the aim direction.
- Let that extra velocity wear off at 1500 px/s² until it reaches zero, separate from normal movement.
- Stack the pushes from rapid fire, but cap the total so the player can't be launched.
- Run the push through normal collision so it never moves the player into a wall or hazard.
- Make the push size a per-weapon setting, with a way to turn it off.

Acceptance checks:
1. One shot moves the player back a few pixels, then they stop.
2. Firing five times quickly moves them back further, up to the cap.
3. Recoil never pushes the player through a wall.
4. With recoil off, shooting does not move the player.

sources.title: Jan Willem Nijman (Vlambeer), "The art of screenshake", INDIGO Classes 2013 (YouTube)
